promptText: Your team updates an authoritative DNS record to redirect away from a failed primary region the instant the failure is detected. Users nonetheless keep hitting the dead region for several more minutes. What is the most likely cause?
options: Resolvers and clients that already cached the previous answer continue serving it until that cached record's TTL expires, independent of how quickly the authoritative server was updated
The root DNS servers must re-propagate the updated record to every TLD server before any client can see the change
The load balancer in the failed region has not yet been restarted, so it keeps intercepting traffic regardless of DNS
DNS updates are rejected by resolvers unless accompanied by a matching TTL decrease at the time of the original record creation
explanation: DNS answers are cached per the record's TTL by resolvers and clients all over the internet; updating the authoritative record does nothing to retroactively invalidate those already-cached answers, so anyone holding a cached answer keeps using it until it naturally expires. This is exactly why failover-relevant records should be configured with short TTLs ahead of time, not after an incident starts.

promptText: A two-region service relies solely on round-robin DNS (multiple A records returned in rotating order) instead of a managed load balancer. One region's backend goes completely down. What happens, concretely?
options: The dead region's IP keeps being handed out in rotation to new DNS queries until someone manually removes the record, and clients that already cached it keep using it until the TTL expires, because round-robin DNS has no concept of backend health
DNS automatically stops returning the dead IP within one query cycle because every resolver re-validates liveness before caching an answer
The remaining healthy region silently absorbs 100% of traffic because round-robin DNS detects the failure and reroutes within seconds
Round-robin DNS requires a minimum of three records, so a two-region setup would have failed configuration validation before this could happen
explanation: Round-robin DNS blindly rotates through configured records with zero health awareness; a dead IP stays in circulation until manually removed, and the usual TTL-caching problem compounds it further. This is precisely the gap that drove the industry toward dedicated, actively health-checked load balancers.

promptText: A cost-conscious team wants to replace their L7 Application Load Balancer with a cheaper Layer 4 Network Load Balancer, keeping identical routing rules that send /api/orders/** and /api/users/** to different backend pools. Why can't an L4 load balancer reproduce this routing on its own?
options: An L4 load balancer only sees transport-layer information (source/destination IP and port, protocol) and never parses the HTTP request, so it has no way to know a URL path even exists, let alone route on it
L4 load balancers can see the URL path but are restricted by RFC to ignoring it for performance reasons
L4 load balancers can only forward UDP traffic, and this API traffic is served over TCP
L4 load balancers require the backend pools to be registered under the same DNS hostname, which path-based routing violates
explanation: Path-based routing requires terminating the connection and reading the actual HTTP request, which is exactly the capability that distinguishes L7 from L4; an L4 load balancer structurally cannot see a URL path because it never progresses past connection-level data.

promptText: A service has instances that are identical in capacity, and nearly all requests take roughly the same amount of time to process. Which load-balancing algorithm is the right default here, and why not reach for something more sophisticated?
options: Round robin, because with uniform request cost and uniform instance capacity its simple equal-count distribution already produces an equal-load distribution, so a more sophisticated algorithm would add measurement and tuning overhead without a corresponding benefit
Latency-aware "power of two choices", because it is always strictly better than round robin regardless of traffic shape
Consistent hashing, because it is required any time more than one backend instance exists
Weighted least connections, because weights are mandatory for any production load balancer configuration
explanation: Round robin's assumption, that equal request counts produce equal load, only holds when request cost and instance capacity are both roughly uniform, which is exactly the case described; reaching for a more complex algorithm here adds operational complexity without addressing any real imbalance.

promptText: An active health check is configured to mark an instance unhealthy after a single failed probe, and healthy again after a single successful probe. What production problem does this invite, and what's the standard fix?
options: A single transient network blip can repeatedly yank a perfectly healthy instance out of and back into rotation (flapping), which itself destabilizes load distribution; the fix is requiring several consecutive failures before ejection and several consecutive successes before re-admission
This configuration is actually optimal because it reacts to failures as fast as theoretically possible with no downside
This only matters for passive health checks, not active ones, so no change is needed here
The fix is to increase the health check's timeout value, which eliminates the need for any threshold at all
explanation: A probe failure can easily be spurious noise rather than a genuine failure; without consecutive-failure/success thresholds, an instance can be ejected and re-admitted repeatedly on noise alone, which is its own source of instability distinct from the slower-failover problem a higher threshold trades against.

promptText: A team enables sticky sessions to keep per-user in-memory session state working correctly. Besides fixing the immediate symptom, what structural cost does this introduce to the system's load balancing?
options: Load can no longer be freely rebalanced away from an instance that accumulates a disproportionate share of sticky users, and if that instance fails, every client pinned to it loses its session-dependent state since no other instance can serve them correctly
Sticky sessions make the load balancer incapable of performing any active health checks on the affected instances
Sticky sessions force every instance to run the exact same application version, blocking rolling deploys permanently
Sticky sessions eliminate the need for a load-balancing algorithm entirely, since routing becomes fully deterministic
explanation: Pinning a client to one instance undermines even load distribution as sticky populations grow unevenly, and more seriously, ties that client's session survival to that one instance's survival, exactly the single-point-of-failure risk load balancing exists to eliminate, which is why externalizing session state is the preferred long-term fix.

promptText: Using Little's Law (L = λ × W), explain why "least connections" routes more effectively than round robin when request processing time varies significantly across requests.
options: For a given arrival rate λ, an instance's active connection count L is directly proportional to average processing time W, so an instance currently handling slower requests naturally accumulates a higher connection count, exactly the signal least connections uses to avoid piling more work onto it
Little's Law proves that round robin and least connections always converge to identical steady-state load distributions over a long enough time window
Little's Law applies only to database connection pools, not to load-balancer-level connection counts, so it cannot justify this algorithm choice
Little's Law shows that λ is irrelevant to connection count, so least connections is really just measuring instance uptime
explanation: Because L = λ × W, holding arrival rate constant, a higher W (slower processing) directly produces a higher L (more active connections) on that instance, which is precisely the real-time signal least connections reacts to; round robin ignores W entirely and can therefore leave load unevenly distributed.

promptText: A canary rollout is configured with the stable version at weight 99 and the new version at weight 1 under weighted round robin, with plans to ramp the canary's weight up gradually. What does this configuration actually guarantee about traffic distribution, and why ramp gradually rather than jumping straight to a 50/50 split?
options: The expected fraction of traffic to each version is its weight divided by the total weight (roughly 1% to the canary initially), and ramping gradually limits the blast radius of a bad canary release before exposing it to a large fraction of real traffic
Weighted round robin guarantees the canary receives exactly 1 out of every 99 requests in strict alternating order, identical to unweighted round robin
A 1/99 weight split means the canary will only receive traffic from a single geographic region, not users at large
Weights in weighted round robin control health-check frequency per instance, not traffic share, so this configuration has no effect on how much traffic the canary sees
explanation: fraction_i = w_i / (sum of weights) is the formula behind proportional traffic shifting; starting the canary at a small weight and ramping it up over time is exactly how a gradual, low-risk rollout is implemented at the load-balancing layer, limiting exposure if the canary turns out to be bad.

promptText: A health check probe has an independent 2% chance of a spurious (transient, not-really-unhealthy) failure. Moving the unhealthy threshold from k=1 to k=3 consecutive failures changes the false-ejection probability from roughly 2% to roughly 0.0008%. What trade-off is being made by increasing k, and why is it usually worth it?
options: Reaction time to a genuinely dead instance gets slightly slower since more consecutive real failures are now required before ejection, but this is traded for a dramatically lower chance of ejecting a perfectly healthy instance due to transient noise, usually a good trade since false ejections cause their own instability
Increasing k has no real trade-off; it only improves false-positive rates with zero cost to detection speed
Increasing k makes the health check cheaper to run because fewer probes are sent overall
Increasing k converts the health check from active to passive, which is a different mechanism entirely
explanation: Because false-ejection probability shrinks roughly as p^k, a higher k sharply reduces spurious ejections, but it necessarily costs some reaction time since a genuinely failing instance now must fail several consecutive probes before being removed, exactly the false-positive-vs-reaction-time dial production systems tune deliberately.

promptText: A Kubernetes pod shows status "Running" and is passing liveness checks, yet the load balancer in front of it keeps sending real user traffic to it even though it lost its database connection minutes ago. What is misconfigured?
options: The load balancer's health check is polling the liveness endpoint instead of the readiness endpoint; liveness only confirms the process hasn't deadlocked, while readiness is the signal meant to reflect whether the instance can actually serve a correct response right now
Nothing is misconfigured, liveness and readiness are two names for the identical check, so this behavior is expected
The pod needs to be manually restarted, since Kubernetes has no mechanism for an orchestrator-level liveness probe at all
The load balancer should be switched from active to passive health checking, which would automatically fix the stale readiness view
explanation: Liveness answers "is the process still running," used by an orchestrator to decide on restarts, while readiness answers "can this instance correctly serve traffic right now" and is what an external load balancer's health check should poll; a readiness check that actually exercises the database connection would have correctly flagged this instance as not-ready.

promptText: A request for a dynamic, per-user API call passes through GeoDNS and then a CDN's edge network before reaching the origin. What is the precise division of labor between these two routing layers?
options: GeoDNS decides which data center or origin the request is ultimately bound for based on the resolver's apparent location, while the CDN's edge network uses its own independent (often anycast-based) routing to intercept and, where possible, serve the request before it ever reaches that origin at all
GeoDNS and CDN edge routing are two marketing names for the exact same mechanism operating at the same layer of the stack
The CDN decides which data center the request is bound for, and GeoDNS only caches static assets once the CDN has already made that decision
GeoDNS only applies to IPv6 clients, while CDN edge routing only applies to IPv4 clients
explanation: DNS (including GeoDNS) resolves which origin a hostname points to before any packet is sent, while a CDN's edge network is a separate, complementary layer that intercepts requests at a point of presence close to the client and can answer directly from cache; conflating the two is a common mistake since they solve different parts of the routing problem.

promptText: In the layered request path, DNS/GeoDNS, external L7 gateway, service mesh sidecar, each layer is deliberately given a different update frequency and granularity for its routing decisions. What's the underlying engineering reason for this structure?
options: The closer a layer sits to the actual workload, the cheaper and faster it is to gather accurate health/load signals, so that layer can be trusted with fine-grained, frequently re-evaluated decisions; layers farther away (DNS being farthest) face expensive, slow signal propagation and are therefore best used only for coarse, slow-changing decisions
The layering is purely historical, there is no technical reason a service mesh sidecar couldn't make the same coarse, infrequent decisions DNS makes instead
Each layer is assigned decisions randomly during infrastructure provisioning to balance configuration load across teams
DNS is given the finest-grained decisions because it is queried most frequently of any layer in the stack
explanation: Signal freshness and propagation cost scale with distance from the workload: a sidecar can cheaply gather second-by-second health data about its one instance, while DNS answers are cached globally for minutes, so the stack deliberately matches decision granularity to how cheaply and quickly each layer can get accurate information.

promptText: A service must meet a 30-second RTO during a full regional failure. A team proposes handling this purely by making the DNS failover automatic (health-check-triggered) and leaving everything else as-is. Why is this insufficient on its own?
options: Even automatic DNS failover cannot help clients already holding a cached answer with a long TTL, and if the secondary region isn't already warm with ready capacity, the time spent cold-starting instances and passing health checks alone could consume most or all of the 30-second budget; the RTO requires short TTLs, automated failover, AND pre-provisioned warm capacity together
Automatic DNS failover alone is always sufficient for any RTO, since health-check-triggered failover happens instantaneously across every resolver globally
The 30-second RTO is unachievable regardless of configuration, since DNS propagation to root servers always takes several minutes at minimum
The only requirement for a 30-second RTO is making the DNS update automatic; TTL values and backend capacity are unrelated to RTO
explanation: A tight RTO is a system property that has to be engineered across every layer coherently: short TTLs on failover-relevant records (since a long cached TTL alone can blow the budget regardless of how fast the record updates), automated rather than manual failover triggering, and warm standby capacity in the secondary region (since cold-starting capacity during the incident consumes time against the same budget); fixing only one of these leaves the RTO unmet.

promptText: An instance is passing all active health checks but a subset of real user requests to it are silently returning degraded results, a "gray failure." Why does a standard binary healthy/unhealthy health-check model fail to catch this, and what kind of signal is needed instead?
options: A binary health check only reflects whatever the specific probe exercises, not real traffic outcomes, so an instance can pass every probe while still serving degraded results to requests the probe doesn't resemble; catching this requires continuous passive monitoring of real traffic (error rates, full latency percentiles, not just averages) rather than tightening the existing binary threshold
Gray failures are impossible to miss with any active health check, so this scenario indicates the health check interval is simply set too infrequently
The fix is always to lower the unhealthy threshold to 1 consecutive failure, which guarantees gray failures are caught immediately
Gray failures only occur in passive health-check systems, so switching entirely to active checks resolves the issue
explanation: Binary health checks exist in a blind spot for gray failures precisely because the probe's narrow pattern doesn't exercise the same code path or conditions that real degraded requests hit; the fix is richer, continuous, traffic-derived signal (real error rates and latency percentiles) rather than adjusting thresholds on the same shallow probe.

promptText: A new external L7 gateway is placed in front of a fleet that already performs client-side load balancing via Spring Cloud LoadBalancer for internal calls. Both layers independently retry failed requests. What specific risk does this combination introduce?
options: Retry amplification: if both the gateway and the client-side balancer independently retry on failure without coordination, a single failing downstream instance can multiply into far more retry traffic than intended, and the two layers may also hold inconsistent views of which instances are healthy at any given moment
No risk is introduced, since Spring Cloud LoadBalancer automatically disables its own retries whenever an upstream gateway is detected
The two layers cannot coexist technically, so requests would fail outright rather than risk retry amplification
The only consequence is slightly higher memory usage on the gateway, with no effect on retry behavior or traffic volume
explanation: Independent, uncoordinated retries at two separate layers compound multiplicatively against a struggling downstream instance, and because each layer forms its own health view on its own timescale, the gateway can keep routing to a pool it believes is healthy while the client-side balancer inside that pool is still routing to an instance the gateway's own check would have already excluded, a double-balancing hazard worth explicitly designing retry budgets and health-view consistency around.
